explanations.explanation: Imagination, baker. God tells His prophet to say to them, “…out of their own imagination: Hear the word of the LORD!” (Ezekiel 13:2). They're talking up a storm, but the words started in their own heads. That's like me swearing a cookie recipe came from heaven when I dreamed it up during a nap.

Traditions sound respectable, friend, but that isn't the word here. God says these prophets prophesy “…out of their own imagination…” (Ezekiel 13:2). The words came from their own imagination. Even a smudged recipe card has more behind it than that.

Scrolls would at least mean somebody wrote something down! But God never mentions a scroll in this verse. He says they prophesy “…out of their own imagination…” (Ezekiel 13:2). The source is their own imagination.

I see why it might look that way, friend, but God says the opposite. He says, “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit yet have seen nothing.” (Ezekiel 13:3). Foolish, not wise. When God starts a sentence with “Woe,” nobody is getting a compliment.

False, and God doesn't dance around it. He says, “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit yet have seen nothing.” (Ezekiel 13:3). Foolish is the word He uses. Following your own spirit and seeing nothing is not a wisdom plan.

Not quite, baker. God says the opposite: “You did not go up to the gaps or restore the wall around the house of Israel…” (Ezekiel 13:5). They did not go up to the gaps, and they did not restore the wall.

False, and God says it plainly. “You did not go up to the gaps or restore the wall around the house of Israel…” (Ezekiel 13:5). They did not go up to the gaps, and they did not restore the wall. All talk, no trowel.

explanations.answer: So it would stand in battle on the Day of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one. God says the wall needed restoring “…so that it would stand in the battle on the Day of the LORD.” (Ezekiel 13:5). It had a job to do on that day. And God says these prophets did not restore it.

explanations.answer: So it would stand through the famine the LORD sends
explanations.explanation: A famine isn't what this verse says, friend. God says the wall needed restoring so it would stand “…in the battle on the Day of the LORD.” (Ezekiel 13:5). A battle, not a famine. A wall is built for the day somebody pushes against it.

explanations.answer: So it would stand when the LORD brings the exiles home
explanations.explanation: I get the guess, friend, but this verse says something else. God says the wall needed restoring “…so that it would stand in the battle on the Day of the LORD.” (Ezekiel 13:5). Nothing here about a homecoming. It's about a wall holding up in battle.

explanations.answer: They wait for it to be fulfilled
explanations.explanation: Yep. The LORD did not send them, “yet they wait for the fulfillment of their message.” (Ezekiel 13:6). They hand out the message and then stand around expecting it to come true. I think that takes some nerve. It's like never turning the oven on and then waiting for the cookies to come out.

explanations.answer: They admit that they made it up
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice twist, baker, but it isn't what the verse says. They claim, “Thus declares the LORD…” when the LORD did not send them (Ezekiel 13:6). Instead, God says “…they wait for the fulfillment of their message.”

explanations.answer: They stop telling it to anyone
explanations.explanation: If only. But God says they “…speak lying divinations.” and claim, “Thus declares the LORD…” (Ezekiel 13:6). They keep right on speaking, and they even wait “…for the fulfillment of their message.” Quiet is the one thing they're not.

That's what He says. “Because you have uttered vain words and seen false visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 13:8). That's heavy, so I'll say it once and plainly. God takes it seriously when people put their own words in His mouth.

Sparing isn't what God says here, friend. He says, “Because you have uttered vain words and seen false visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 13:8). That's a serious line. Vain words and false visions are what bring it on.

I wish this verse said that, baker, but it doesn't. God says, “Because you have uttered vain words and seen false visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 13:8). No forgiveness is offered in this verse. It's a hard one, and I think it's meant to be.

True. God says they will not “…be recorded in the register of the house of Israel…” (Ezekiel 13:9). They also won't belong to the council of His people or enter the land of Israel. That's a lot of doors closing at once.

It's actually true, baker. God says these prophets will not belong to the council of His people or “…be recorded in the register of the house of Israel…” (Ezekiel 13:9). They won't enter the land of Israel either. Their names won't be on the list.

Peace is it, baker. God says they led His people astray, “…saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace…” (Ezekiel 13:10). The same verse says they were whitewashing any flimsy wall that was built. One soothing word, and there was no peace behind it.

Repent would be a different word entirely, friend. Repent isn't the word in this verse. God says these prophets led His people astray “…saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace…” (Ezekiel 13:10). The word they gave was peace.

If they'd said flee, people might have moved. But God says they led His people astray “…saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace…” (Ezekiel 13:10). The message was calm and comforting. It just wasn't true.
Whitewash is the word. God says they were “…whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built…” (Ezekiel 13:10). A fresh coat of white on a weak wall. It looks sturdy right up until the weather shows up.

Walking away would almost be more honest, baker. But God says they were “…whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built…” (Ezekiel 13:10). They didn't leave it alone. They painted it and made it look good.

Guarding a wall is real work, friend, and that's not what these prophets are doing. God says they were “…whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built…” (Ezekiel 13:10). They were whitewashing it, not guarding it.

Other way around, baker. God tells Ezekiel, “…tell those whitewashing the wall that it will fall.” (Ezekiel 13:11). Rain will come in torrents, hailstones will plunge down, and a windstorm will burst forth. That wall isn't standing.
False. God says, “…tell those whitewashing the wall that it will fall.” (Ezekiel 13:11). It's not a comfortable message, but it's the true one. A wall that falls doesn't care how nice it looked.

That's the list. “Rain will come in torrents, I will send hailstones plunging down, and a windstorm will burst forth.” (Ezekiel 13:11). Three kinds of weather, and one flimsy wall. Paint doesn't hold up in that.

Soldiers is a fair guess for a wall, friend, but not here. God says, “Rain will come in torrents, I will send hailstones plunging down, and a windstorm will burst forth.” (Ezekiel 13:11). The attackers are weather, not an army. No Egypt in this verse.

A quake would certainly do the job, baker. But God names something else: “Rain will come in torrents, I will send hailstones plunging down, and a windstorm will burst forth.” (Ezekiel 13:11). Rain, hail and wind. The ground isn't mentioned shaking.

True. God says, “I will tear down the wall you whitewashed and level it to the ground, so that its foundation is exposed.” (Ezekiel 13:14). Not just cracked, but level to the ground. And all that whitewash goes down with it.

It's true, baker. God says, “I will tear down the wall you whitewashed and level it to the ground, so that its foundation is exposed.” (Ezekiel 13:14). The wall comes all the way down. Nothing is left standing to paint.

The city, yes. God says, “The city will fall, and you will be destroyed within it.” (Ezekiel 13:14). It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to land that way. Then He adds, “Then you will know that I am the Lord…”

The temple is a big building, friend, but this verse never mentions it. God says, “The city will fall, and you will be destroyed within it.” (Ezekiel 13:14). It's the city that falls. Stick with what the verse names.

There's no tower in this verse, baker. God says, “The city will fall, and you will be destroyed within it.” (Ezekiel 13:14). The wall comes down, and the city falls too. It's a bigger fall than one tower.

Not quite, friend. After the storm, God says He will tell them, “The wall is gone, and so are those who whitewashed it…” (Ezekiel 13:15). That comes after He has vented His wrath against the wall and against those who whitewashed it. The wall is gone, and so are they.

False. God says, “The wall is gone, and so are those who whitewashed it…” (Ezekiel 13:15). He names them as the prophets of Israel who saw a vision of peace for Jerusalem when there was no peace. The wall and the whitewashers are both gone.

Not at all, baker. God tells His prophet, “Prophesy against them” (Ezekiel 13:17). He is to set his face against the daughters of his people who prophesy out of their own imagination. These women get a word from God too.

False. God tells His prophet to set his face against these women and says, “Prophesy against them” (Ezekiel 13:17). So he has something to say to them. It starts with “Woe to the women who sew magic charms on their wrists…” (Ezekiel 13:18).
That's the reason God gives. These women sew charms and make veils “…in order to ensnare their souls.” (Ezekiel 13:18). The charms and veils are made to trap people. Nothing gentle about it.

I wish that were it, baker, but God says the opposite. These women sew charms and make veils “…in order to ensnare their souls.” (Ezekiel 13:18). It's about trapping people. Honor doesn't come into it.

Mourning would be a sad but understandable reason, friend. God gives a different one: these charms and veils are made “…in order to ensnare their souls.” (Ezekiel 13:18). That's a trap, not grief. The verse mentions no mourning at all.

explanations.answer: Handfuls of barley and scraps of bread
explanations.explanation: That's the price. God says, “You have profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread.” (Ezekiel 13:19). Handfuls and scraps. That's a small payment for such a big wrong.

explanations.answer: Pieces of silver and bars of gold
explanations.explanation: Silver and gold would at least be a big payday, baker, but that's not what the verse says. God says, “You have profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread.” (Ezekiel 13:19). Barley and bread, nothing shiny. It's about as small as a payoff gets.

explanations.answer: Fine linen robes and gold jewelry
explanations.explanation: Fancy clothes and jewelry would be a bigger prize, friend. God names a smaller one: “You have profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread.” (Ezekiel 13:19). Barley and scraps of bread. No robes in sight.

True, and it's a hard line. God says that by lying to My people who would listen, “…you have killed those who should not have died and spared those who should not have lived.” (Ezekiel 13:19). Their lies pointed life and death the wrong way. I think this one hurts.

It's true, baker. God says, “…you have killed those who should not have died and spared those who should not have lived.” (Ezekiel 13:19). That came from lying to His people who would listen. I think this verse is hard to hear.
Set free, baker. God says, “So I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds.” (Ezekiel 13:20). He tears the charms from their arms and the trap opens. Good news after a hard passage.

Judgment is in this chapter, friend, but that's not what God says here about these souls. God says, “So I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds.” (Ezekiel 13:20). The trapped ones are the ones He frees.
Thankfully, no. God says, “So I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds.” (Ezekiel 13:20). He tears the charms away and sets those souls loose. Nobody stays in that trap.

Righteous goes in the first blank. God says, “Because you have disheartened the righteous with your lies, even though I have caused them no grief…” (Ezekiel 13:22). People who were doing right got discouraged by lies. That's heavy, and God calls it out.

Wicked goes in the second blank. God says they “…encouraged the wicked not to turn from their evil ways to save their lives…” (Ezekiel 13:22). So the lies disheartened the righteous and encouraged the wicked to keep to their evil ways.
Priests aren't mentioned in this verse, baker. God says they disheartened “the righteous” and encouraged “the wicked” (Ezekiel 13:22). Those two groups go in the blanks.
Exiles isn't a word this verse uses, friend. God says these women disheartened “the righteous” and encouraged “the wicked” (Ezekiel 13:22). Those are the two words that fit the blanks.
Elders isn't a word this verse uses, baker. God says they disheartened “the righteous” and encouraged “the wicked” (Ezekiel 13:22). The blanks are for those two.

None at all. God says these women disheartened the righteous “…with your lies, even though I have caused them no grief…” (Ezekiel 13:22). The hurt came from the lies, not from Him. He's careful to say so.

Not even a little, baker. God says they disheartened the righteous with lies, “…even though I have caused them no grief…” (Ezekiel 13:22). No grief from Him at all. The discouragement came from the lies.
The verse says the reverse, friend. God says the righteous were disheartened with lies, “…even though I have caused them no grief…” (Ezekiel 13:22). He caused no grief at all. The lies caused it.
